blogs.title: Digital Delivery and 'Receipt': How the Fifth Circuit Navigates Automated Insurance Cancellations Under Strict State Statutes
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Fifth Circuit's handling of modern technological realities versus rigid statutory language in *Williams v. GoAuto*. It focuses on the court's interpretation of 'receipt' under Louisiana law, specifically addressing whether an automated email triggering a computer-based cancellation constitutes valid 'receipt' by the insurer before human intervention occurs. The analysis explores the tension between the doctrine of 'strict adherence' required for insurance cancellations and the practicalities of high-volume, algorithm-driven business operations, concluding why the court rejected the plaintiffs' argument that a human must physically possess the document for cancellation to be effective.

blogs.title: To Sign or Not to Sign? The Absence of Judicial Authority on Corporate Certifications in Premium Finance Law
blogs.description: Focusing on the procedural requirement of 'certification,' this blog examines the Fifth Circuit's decision that a corporate seal or signature is not legally mandated for a premium finance company to effectuate cancellation. The post discusses how the court navigated sparse Louisiana precedent, distinguishing cases where unsigned notices were deemed insufficient due to other defects rather than the lack of a signature alone. It critiques the court's reluctance to read implicit requirements into an express statute and considers the broader implication: that corporate entities may satisfy statutory 'certification' duties through standardized digital assertions without individual employee identification.

blogs.title: Reluctance to Leap: Why Federal Courts Will Decline Certification Even Amidst Ambiguous State Insurance Law
blogs.description: This article centers on the appellate court's refusal to certify questions regarding statutory interpretation to the Louisiana Supreme Court despite acknowledged ambiguity in state case law. Drawing on Fifth Circuit jurisprudence (specifically *Jefferson*), it analyzes why mere legislative silence or lower-court confusion is insufficient grounds for certification. The post evaluates whether this approach risks creating federal common law interpretations that diverge from potential future state rulings and discusses the strategic implications for litigants seeking clarity in cross-border commercial disputes involving state-specific regulatory schemes.
